newsitem.title: UK: Scottish food poisoning among world's worst.
newsitem.headline: Scottish food poisoning among world's worst.

text.p: Scotland's outbreak of E coli food poisoning is among the worst such cases ever recorded, British health officials said on Thursday. The 11 fatalities have all been elderly and most are linked to two butcher shops in Scotland. Several children have also been given dialysis treatment in hospital.

More than 300 people have reported symptoms of the food poisoning, which can cause kidney failure in vulnerable people such as the elderly and young children. Doctors have confirmed more than 200 cases and say the number has stabilised.

"This is further evidence that the worst of the outbreak is over and that the control measures we have implemented are working," said Dr Syed Ahmed, an expert in public health medicine at the Lanarkshire Health Board.
The poisoning first appeared among pensioners attending a lunch and was traced to meat pies supplied by an award-winning Scottish butcher in Lanarkshire.
A second, smaller outbreak in the neighbouring Forth valley has not been linked to the shop, although deaths there are counted in the Scottish total.

The deadliest outbreak of E coli was in Canada, where 19 elderly people infected in a nursing home died in September 1985. More than 70 people reported symptoms, Britain's Advisory Committee on Microbiological Safety of Food said.
Eleven people, mostly schoolchildren, died in an outbreak in Japan in July and 9,500 became ill.
In 1993, an outbreak linked to hamburgers sold by a U.S. fast-food chain caused an international outcry. One child died and hundreds of people were affected.
There have been several deaths this year in Washington state, Colorado, California and Canada linked to unpasteurised apple juice.
E coli is a bacteria normally found in the guts of cattle, sheep and people. It is usually harmless but one strain, known as 0157, can cause brain damage and kidney failure.
It gets into food via improper slaughtering techniques or through manure used as fertiliser.
E coli poisoning was first identified in 1982 in the United States.
